entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of LLM-JEPA
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract was good overall and conveyed the main message clearly. I added a brief explanation of how JEPA predicts the embedding of one view from another, along with a concrete example from language: a natural-language description paired with its corresponding code. This helps readers who are unfamiliar with JEPA understand the proposed approach on a first read.

Before and after

Before

Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, finetuning, and evaluation rely on input-space reconstruction and generative capabilities. Yet, it has been observed in vision that embedding-space training objectives, e.g., with Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), are far superior to their input-space counterpart. That mismatch in how training is achieved between language and vision opens up a natural question: can language training methods learn a few tricks from the vision ones? The lack of JEPA-style LLM is a testimony of the challenge in designing such objectives for language. In this work, we propose a first step in that direction where we develop LLM-JEPA, a JEPA based solution for LLMs applicable both to finetuning and pretraining. Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform the standard LLM training objectives by a significant margin across models, all while being robust to overfiting. Those findings are observed across numerous datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes) and various models from the Llama3, OpenELM, Gemma2 and Olmo families.

After

Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained to predict the next token in a text sequence. In vision, training objectives defined in embedding space have outperformed input-space reconstruction in some settings. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) use this approach by predicting the embedding of one view from another. We introduce LLM-JEPA, a training objective that applies this principle to LLM pretraining and fine-tuning using paired views such as a natural-language description and its corresponding code. Across experiments on NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, and Rotten Tomatoes, LLM-JEPA outperforms standard training objectives across models from the Llama 3, OpenELM, Gemma 2, and OLMo families and shows robustness to overfitting.

The general rule

When an abstract borrows a method from another field, explain what the method does in one sentence and give a concrete example from the new setting.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.

entry.title: Week 5 in one page: Spurious Forgetting

link.title: Week 5 in one page: Spurious Forgetting

entry.content:
About the paper

Finetune an LLM on new facts and it often seems to forget what it knew before. Previous work showed that some of this forgetting is spurious: the old knowledge is still in the model, just hidden, and can be recovered. This paper asks when and why that happens. It finds that recall of old facts can collapse, then come back on its own as training continues, before a slower, permanent erosion sets in. The authors identify three ingredients for the spurious part: old facts queried in similar ways, new answers concentrated in one part of the vocabulary, and a normalization layer.

Our posts:

✍️ Writing. Rewriting the abstract puts the paper’s main point first, that forgetting during finetuning is two processes and only one is permanent, and replaces unexplained jargon with plain language. A copyedit of Section 2 introduces the two settings and the experiment before the results, shows the evidence that the old knowledge is hidden, not erased, and ends with the questions the experiment raises.

🧠 Learning. To understand how a model can lose access to facts without erasing them, we first look at where facts are stored. The post summarizes work showing that a transformer’s feed-forward layers act like key-value memories: each neuron detects a pattern in the input and pushes the model toward certain next words, and the final prediction combines many such memories.

📊 Visualization. A better Figure 1 removes redundancy: since one finetuning scenario is a special case of the other, it keeps a single panel and cleans up the rest, labeling the lines directly and shading the pretraining phase as context. Two redesigns of Figure 3 then explain why old facts come back: a schematic of the three phases, with and without normalization, showing where old and new facts land and which are answered, and an interactive story in which a shared shortcut helps the model learn the new facts but hides the old ones, then becomes harmful, so training pulls it back and the old facts reappear without being retrained. Two redesigns of Figure 5 show the evidence that removing a single direction restores old facts: grouped bars make the size of the recovery easy to compare against a random-direction control, and a redesign with one panel per experiment draws ordinary finetuning and the edit side by side, and adds the cost of the edit on the new facts, which the original left out.

🔬 Research. A literature review places the paper where four lines of work meet, from catastrophic forgetting to recoverable forgetting, and points to the paper that coined “spurious forgetting” as the one to read first. Two posts follow the authors’ path, one on Palit and Schölkopf and one on all five authors, from interpretability, causality and the study of how models learn facts to this paper. Two critiques ask how far the results go: one on the toy model questions whether the simplified model and synthetic data match real LLMs, and the other on the OLMo results asks why OLMo recovered old facts in only one of two experiments and proposes a cleaner test. Three follow-ups propose experiments on semantic structure, abilities beyond facts, and preventing the shift through training order.

💻 Coding. A ten-seed reproduction of Figure 2 rebuilds the paper’s toy memory and shows that the more the facts share, the sharper the collapse of old facts, followed by recovery and erosion. A rerun of Figure 1 reproduces the paper’s two finetuning scenarios, then rewrites the new facts in a different phrasing and finds that the wording changes what gets forgotten, and that the paper’s explanation does not cover every case.

🔭 Scouting. The scouting posts look for recent work on the paper’s question: when is lost knowledge really gone? Five papers on forgetting during finetuning start from the paper that named spurious forgetting and cover why reinforcement learning forgets less, when replay is enough, and how pretraining length matters. Two posts find the same pattern of hidden, not erased knowledge elsewhere: facts removed by editing a model can still be read from inside it, and information supposedly removed by unlearning hides in intermediate layers. Two more look at ways to forget less, such as deleting a tiny fraction of weights, and at a trend where much of “training” turns out to be a single shift, which echoes the paper’s shared shift.

📣 Communication. An eight-post X thread explains spurious forgetting, its mechanism and the class’s experiments, and connects it to machine unlearning, with an earlier X post inviting discussion. A post on AIDA shows how to structure slide posts (attention, interest, desire, action), with a Canva template, and the slides were also posted on Instagram and TikTok.
entry.summary: Our focus points from a paper on when forgetting during finetuning is not catastrophic.

entry.title: Does learning to write a regex also align its embedding?

link.title: Does learning to write a regex also align its embedding?

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

I reimplemented the right panel of Figure 3 with a small Transformer trained on NL-RX-SYNTH, the paper’s English-to-regex dataset. Paper, §3.3 and Figure 3

I measured next-token prediction (NTP) loss and JEPA loss, which measures the cosine distance between independently encoded prompts and regexes. The baseline trained on NTP alone and still tracked JEPA loss. The second condition trained on both losses. Each condition ran for 300 updates with five matched seeds.

The code

Experiment script

Results

What I learned

Adding JEPA lowered the embedding loss from 1.277 in the baseline to 0.013 over the final five updates. NTP loss fell in both conditions and finished higher with JEPA (0.635 vs. 0.492 nats). The paper’s NTP curves nearly overlap. Paper, Figure 3

entry.title: New abstract for LLM-JEPA
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract is fairly good, actually! In the sense that, at least, i understood some what they were trying to convery in the paper (as opposed to some previous papers we’ve read recently). Another benefit is that it’s actually pretty short and to the point. Having said that, i felt that the abstract, and the paper as a whole, has some JEPA-optimistic bias (which i get!). I tried to rewrite it in a somewhat more balanced way.

Yann (et al)’s version:

Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, finetuning, and evaluation rely on input-space reconstruction and generative capabilities. Yet, it has been observed in vision that embedding-space training objectives, e.g., with Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), are far superior to their input-space counterpart. That mismatch in how training is achieved between language and vision opens up a natural question: can language training methods learn a few tricks from the vision ones? The lack of JEPA-style LLM is a testimony of the challenge in designing such objectives for language. In this work, we propose a first step in that direction where we develop LLM-JEPA, a JEPA based solution for LLMs applicable both to finetuning and pretraining. Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform the standard LLM training objectives by a significant margin across models, all while being robust to overfiting. Those findings are observed across numerous datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes) and various models from the Llama3, OpenELM, Gemma2 and Olmo families.

My Version:

Nowadays, State-of-the-art LLMs are pretrained almost exclusively on a single task - autoregressive text prediction. This loss, powerful as it may be, does not explicitly influence the shape of the representation space. JEPA architerctures, which have shown some favorable results in Vision tasks, focus on shaping the representation space of the inputs. This paper aims to bridge the two. To do so, we offer a combined LLM-JEPA loss, along with small changes to transformer architecture and inputs. We show some gains ranging from modest to substantial, in various models and downstream tasks.

Additional thoughts

The title is good, too, in my opinion. I intentionally removed some of the specifications of the implementation. Besides making it easier to read, my thought was that the readers belong to one of two crowds: (i) familiar with JEPA, in which case the combination is easier to imagine and would want to see the details directly, or (ii) unfamiliar with it, in which they need some background which the asbtract shouldn’t supply. In both cases, leaving it less specific felt more natural to me.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
Cosine Misleads: Auxiliary Losses Reshape Vision Language Models, Not Their Latents

XiuYu Zhang, Junfeng Fang, Zhenkai Liang, 2026.

This paper investigates whether improving the alignment between intermediate latent representations and their target visual embeddings actually improves vision-language model (VLM) performance. This directly addresses a concern raised by LLM-JEPA: forcing related representations to align does not necessarily benefit the model's original task and may even hurt its performance. Their findings suggest that auxiliary representation losses may influence performance by modifying the model's shared parameters rather than by improving the representations used for reasoning.

Next-Latent Prediction Transformers Learn Compact World Models

Jayden Teoh, Manan Tomar, Kwangjun Ahn, Edward S. Hu, Tim Pearce, Pratyusha Sharma, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Riashat Islam, Alex Lamb, John Langford, 2026.

This paper introduces NextLat, an auxiliary training objective that encourages Transformers to predict their next hidden state from the current hidden state and the next token. The goal is to encourage the model to maintain compact internal representations that capture information necessary for future predictions, rather than relying entirely on attention over previous tokens. The authors theoretically show that, under ideal conditions, these hidden states become sufficient for predicting future sequences. This presents another approach to incorporating representation learning into a model's loss function, using the prediction of future hidden states rather than aligning representations of semantically related inputs.
entry.summary: two papers ont the use of hidden representation on the training.

entry.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS MEET JOINT EMBEDDING PREDICTIVE ARCHITECTURES

link.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS MEET JOINT EMBEDDING PREDICTIVE ARCHITECTURES

entry.content:
Weaknesses

Writing and notation. Apart from grammatical errors, the notation has been incoherent. Specifically, Pred(Enc(TEXT)) implies that Pred operates on a single vector, whereas it actually operates on the whole token sequence.

Figure 3 (right). This figure serves as a supporting evidence to the use of the JEPA loss term. It has several flaws:

  1. The figure is underspecified. What is the value of k? What is the x axis, and what magnitudes of x values are seen in the figure?
  2. The comparison is misleading for k>0. For nonzero k, the baseline is evaluated on tokens which it didn’t train on - recall that the training for NTP does not include the [PRED] token. Therefore the observed loss may reflect an untrained prediction mechanism rather than a deficiency in the representations learned by the baseline model. There’s also a mathematical argument that explains why the values of the loss when k>0 are around 1. Because the embedding of [PRED] is randomly initialized, and never changes during training, the final-layer representation also has certain distribution properties. Assuming ‘random in random out’, when modeling the output embedding is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, the expected cosine-similarity between this vector and another vector is 0, and the loss 1. NOTE: inspecting the source code reveals that the default is k=0, but it’s unclear how the experiment was run.
  3. Doesn’t rule out the possibility that the baseline exhibits relative positive vs. negative separation. The JEPA loss takes into account only ‘positive’ pairs, and measures the degree to which the embeddings of pair elements are close in the latent space. It doesn’t take into account whether ‘negative’ pairs induce distant embeddings. Hence, we can’t rule out from the figure (or anywhere else in the paper, as far as I know) that the baseline yields high separation in negative pairs, relative to the separation it yields on positive pairs. It could be that during training, the separation on negative pairs only grows while the separation of positive pairs stays put.
  4. Poor task diversity. The evaluation is done over one specific task of regex generation. It’s unclear whether the JEPA loss is required only for this task, and whether other tasks NTP objective better captures the aims of JEPA.

Flaws in to evaluations. They evaluate the models during and after training.

  1. NL-RX-SYNTH (regex). The way a given output is scored against the ground truth is flawed. Recall the task: the input is a natural language description of a regular expression, and the output should be the regular expression described by the input. Given a predicted regular expression, it is compared by string equality to the ground truth regex. There are multiple (infinite…) ways to write regular expressions for the same regular language. Perhaps the baseline model has certain regex styles it learned from the NTP objective, which is wrongly flagged incorrect.
  2. Rotten Tomatoes. A dataset for the binary classification task of determining the sentiment (Bad/Good) of a movie review. (A) to determine whether the prediction is correct, the first generated token should be the ground truth label. There could be FNs in the scores. The two accuracy results between baseline (56.5%) and LLM-JEPA (57.7%) are very close to one another, as well as to random chance (50%). Without error analysis, it’s hard to infer improvement from this result. (B) only accuracy is reported; a confusion matrix could’ve been insightful.

Unclear contribution of different k values. Figure 7 shows benchmarks using different k values. There’s no clear evidence that certain values of k are generally better than others.

  1. In some cases, k=0 gives better/comparable results to larger values. This calls into question the practical benefits of the additional nonlinear processing provided by predictor tokens.
  2. Why is larger k more important on some tasks but not others? Is there a certain task type that most benefits from larger k?
  3. Whether and how the benefits of large k diminish on longer tasks? Where longer means that the input given to the model is larger.

Underspecification of the negative pair attempt. The authors say they tried training using negative samples as well, with the InfoNCE loss, and got worse results. It doesn’t fit with the intuition, and hence should have been expanded upon in detail. Key knowledge missing: 1) how many negative samples per positive sample was used in a single step? 2) what negatives did they choose, and how difficult were they?

How it could have been improved

Figure 3 (right). 1) Label both axes 2) state k value 3) separate it into two graphs one per evaluated loss 4) add evaluation over (hard) negative pairs as well 5) evaluate over multiple datasets with differing characteristics (and come up with a satisfactory definition of ‘characteristics’)

Evaluations: NL-RX-SYNTH. Instead of string equality, compare the predicted and ground truth regular expressions in terms of the languages they capture. There are algorithms that decide whether two regular expressions have the same language.

Evaluations: Rotten tomatoes. (1) Do error analysis. Show that we don’t need to worry about mis-deserializations. (2) provide confusion matrices.

Effects of k. (1) try to understand which tasks demand large/small k, maybe one may characterize them. (2) fix large k, vary evaluation datasets by length (need to keep the same task though), find out the diminishing returns rule.

Verdict

While the paper does propose and test a direction worth pursuing, I wouldn’t accept the paper as is.
entry.summary: Necessity of JEPA-loss via Fig 3 is flawed; effect of different k values unclear

entry.title: The core idea: a shortcut that helps, until it hurts

link.title: The core idea: a shortcut that helps, until it hurts

entry.content:
How the paper shows it

Figure 3 of the paper explains why recall of the old facts collapses and then recovers on its own. It has three panels: the old facts’ hidden states projected on the shared direction, the size of the common shift s during fine-tuning (with and without normalization), and the shared and individual margins of the new facts.

Everything is there, but the reader has to bring Eq. 5 to decode it. The turning point of the story, the moment the shift starts to hurt the new facts, appears only as the individual margin γ̄ind crossing zero in the right panel. And no panel shows what any of this does to the answer of a single fact.

The redesign

A shared shortcut helps new learning but hides old knowledge. Once precise learning takes over, the shortcut becomes harmful, and retracts. Press Watch the story, or jump between the stages.

What did we just see?

Early in training, the model finds a shortcut: boosting all B answers helps it learn new facts, even before it can distinguish their correct answers. But this shared boost also affects old facts, hiding their correct answers without erasing the underlying information.

The key is RMSNorm. As the shared component grows, normalization weakens the fact-specific signals. Initially, this helps by suppressing misleading signals. Later, once the new associations become accurate, the same effect becomes harmful: the shared boost reduces the score difference between correct and incorrect B answers.

Gradient descent therefore pulls the shared component back. As a side effect, the old facts become accessible again, without ever being retrained.

Not everything comes back

The shared shift can retract: it hid the old fact without erasing it. But a second, slower process is not. Small fact-specific changes keep accumulating and gradually erase some old facts for good. The paper calls this erosion, and only this part is truly catastrophic forgetting.

What changed and why

  • Answers instead of hidden-state geometry, so “the model now answers wrong” is visible directly.
  • One purple lift, identical in both rows, so the shared shift reads as a single object that grows and shrinks.
  • A dashed outline for the stored signal, so hidden and erased look different.

The bars are a qualitative schematic of the mechanism, not measured logits. The curve of the shared lift comes from a simulation of the paper’s minimal model (§3.1; d = 128, α = 0.5, one seed); the code is in minimal_model.py.
entry.summary: Why old facts vanish and come back without retraining, in one picture: a shortcut that helps the new facts, until it hurts them.
